title: Impact of Overtime Eligibility Expansion on Work Hours

llm_response.content:
## 1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID).  
Why: We observe two groups (treated versus controls) over two periods (pre- and post-policy). The treatment is a discrete policy shock that only affects the treated group after implementation, making DID the canonical design.  

Key Assumptions  
1. Parallel-trends: In the absence of the overtime-eligibility expansion, the mean log-hours of treated and control workers would have evolved in parallel.  
2. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers across units).  
3. No other contemporaneous shock differentially hitting the treated group exactly at the policy date.  

Under these assumptions, the coefficient on treat_x_post is the Average Treatment Effect on the Treated (ATT) in log-hours.  

## 2. R Code
```r
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# Difference-in-Differences: Overtime Eligibility Expansion
# -----------------------------------------------------------

# Install packages if missing
need <- setdiff(c("readr", "dplyr", "fixest", "broom"), rownames(installed.packages()))
if (length(need) > 0) install.packages(need, repos = "https://cloud.r-project.org")

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(fixest)
library(broom)

# 1. Read the data -----------------------------------------------------------
df <- read_csv("experiments/exp_b/data/s32_data.csv",
               col_types = cols())

# Sanity check: create interaction if it is not there -----------------------
if (!"treat_x_post" %in% names(df)) {
  df <- df %>% mutate(treat_x_post = treated * post)
}

# 2. Baseline DID (pooled OLS with common time & group effects) -------------
did_ols <- lm(y ~ treated + post + treat_x_post, data = df)
cat("\n== Baseline DID (OLS) ==================================\n")
print(tidy(did_ols))

# 3. Two-way fixed-effects DID (unit & period FE, clustered SE) -------------
did_twfe <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period, 
                  data = df, cluster = "unit_id")
cat("\n== TWFE DID (unit & time FE, clustered) ================\n")
print(summary(did_twfe, se = "cluster"))   # clustered at unit level

# 4. Effect in percentage terms ---------------------------------------------
att_log  <- coef(did_twfe)["treat_x_post"]
att_perc <- (exp(att_log) - 1) * 100
cat(sprintf("\nATT (log-points): %0.4f\nATT (%% change in hours): %0.2f%%\n",
            att_log, att_perc))

# 5. Basic robustness checks -------------------------------------------------
# 5a. Pre-trend placebo: restrict to pre-period only and assign a fake "post"
df_pre  <- df %>% filter(post == 0) %>% 
           mutate(fake_post = ifelse(period == min(period), 0, 1),
                  fake_x     = treated * fake_post)

placebo <- lm(y ~ treated + fake_post + fake_x, data = df_pre)
cat("\n== Placebo (pre-trend falsification) ===================\n")
print(tidy(placebo)["fake_x", ])

# 5b. Alternative SE clustering at treatment group (two clusters) -----------
# Cluster by treated status
did_twfe_grp <- feols(y ~ treat_x_post | unit_id + period, 
                      data = df, cluster = ~treated)
cat("\n== TWFE with clustering by treatment status ============\n")
print(summary(did_twfe_grp))

# End of script --------------------------------------------------------------
```

The script:
1. Loads the CSV file.  
2. Runs the classical DID (OLS) and a two-way fixed-effects DID with unit & period fixed effects, clustering at the individual level.  
3. Prints the ATT both in log-points and as a percentage change in hours.  
4. Performs two simple robustness checks:  
   • Placebo interaction within the pre-period to detect any pre-trend.  
   • Re-estimation with clustering by treatment status instead of by unit.  

Executing the code will generate all numerical results in the console.

## 3. Expected Findings  
Economic intuition suggests the expansion of overtime pay raises employers’ marginal cost of longer hours for newly eligible workers. Firms often respond by cutting overtime hours, re-allocating tasks, or hiring additional labor. Therefore, I expect:

• Sign: Negative coefficient on treat_x_post.  
• Magnitude: Roughly −0.05 to −0.10 log-points, implying a 5 – 10 % reduction in hours for the treated employees after the reform.  

A significant, negative ATT of this size would align with existing evidence on similar overtime policy changes in the U.S.

_ground_truth.identification_strategy: Compare changes in log hours worked before and after the policy change between treated and untreated groups.
_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: The expansion of overtime eligibility significantly increased the log hours worked.
